1 — The Name “Muʿtazila” in History
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02129

The words “withdrawal” (iʿtizāl) and “Muʿtazila” appeared many times in the history of political and intellectual conflict in Islam before the group now known by that name came into existence. By the end of the first Islamic century, in the late seventh century CE, the name “Muʿtazila” had become firmly attached to this particular group. From then on, “Muʿtazilism” referred to a school with its own distinctive views on several basic questions of Islamic belief, as well as its own rational method for dealing with those questions.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02130

The name “Muʿtazila,” then, did not begin with this group. It had already been used more than half a century earlier. We are not talking here, of course, about the linguistic origin of the word, but about when it entered the political and intellectual language of Islam.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02131

It may first have been used in this sense for a number of the Prophet’s Companions who remained neutral during the Battle of the Camel in 36 AH/656 CE, fought between ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib on one side and Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, and ʿĀʾisha bint Abī Bakr, the Prophet’s wife, on the other. The same men also remained neutral during the Battle of Ṣiffīn between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya in 38 AH/658 CE. It was said that they had “withdrawn” from ʿAlī: they refused both to fight him and to fight his enemies.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02132
In a historical report preserved by al-Ṭabarī, the term is actually used for some of these neutral men by Qays ibn Saʿd, ʿAlī’s governor of Egypt. In a letter to ʿAlī, he writes:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02133

“There are men here who have withdrawn from the conflict. They have asked me to leave them alone and let them remain as they are until the affairs of the people are settled”—that is, until the political conflict reaches some kind of resolution—“and then we will see what we think and they will see what they think. I have therefore decided to leave them alone, not to rush into fighting them, and in the meantime to try to win them over. Perhaps God will turn their hearts and lead them away from their error, if He wills.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02134

Other sources also explicitly use the name “Muʿtazila” in the sense of withdrawing from allegiance to ʿAlī. These include the histories of Abū al-Fidāʾ and Ibn al-Athīr, al-Dīnawarī’s The Long Histories, and al-Nawbakhtī’s The Shīʿite Sects. Al-Nawbakhtī’s account is especially worth quoting because he was himself a historian of the Shīʿite sects.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02135
Writing about those who had pledged allegiance to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, he says:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02136

“They later split into three groups. One remained loyal to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, peace be upon him. Another withdrew with Saʿd ibn Mālik. These were Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Muḥammad ibn Maslama al-Anṣārī, and Usāma ibn Zayd ibn Ḥāritha al-Kalbī, the client of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family. These men withdrew from ʿAlī and refused either to fight him or to fight alongside him after having pledged allegiance to him. They were therefore called the Muʿtazila, and they became the forebears of the Muʿtazila for all time.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02137

Nor was this name used only for that first group of neutrals. Later, it was also applied to another group among the followers of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī. After ʿAlī’s death and the founding of the Umayyad caliphate and state by Muʿāwiya, these men “withdrew” from both al-Ḥasan and Muʿāwiya. They believed that Muʿāwiya had begun to rule the Muslims as he pleased, while al-Ḥasan had made peace with him and given up his right to the imamate, as we discussed earlier. This group therefore turned away from political conflict altogether and devoted itself to worship and the reading of the Qurʾān.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02138
2 — Between One “Muʿtazila” and Another
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02139
We can see, then, that the term “Muʿtazila” existed before the later Muʿtazilites established their fully developed rationalist school toward the end of Umayyad rule.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02140
But this raises a question. Among modern researchers, Aḥmad Amīn was the first to draw serious attention to it:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02141
Was there any connection between the “Muʿtazila” of the earliest Islamic period and the later “Muʿtazila” of the final Umayyad period who founded the school we now know by that name?
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02142

With the eye of an alert historian, Aḥmad Amīn identifies the historical line connecting these two Muʿtazilas. In our view, he is right both in identifying that connection and in explaining what made it distinctive.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02143
Looking at the issues over which the Battles of the Camel and Ṣiffīn were fought, Aḥmad Amīn writes that they were:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02144

“Political questions, all revolving around the killing of ʿUthmān and those who killed him, the demand for punishment, his right to the caliphate, Muʿāwiya and whether he had a stronger claim to the caliphate than ʿAlī, and similar matters. The divisions among people over these questions were divisions between political parties. But it is also true that, in that period, every issue—whether social, economic, political, or personal—was given a religious coloring.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
en-ref-V2-180-1
He continues:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02145

“The party or group that was called the ‘Muʿtazila’ in the earliest period represented a political idea expressed in religious terms. If we wanted to sum up its position in a single statement, we could say this: it believed that neither of the two opposing sides clearly had justice on its side. Both were in the wrong, or at the very least it had not become clear which side was right. Religion commands us to fight the side that commits aggression. But if both sides are aggressors, or if we do not know which side is the aggressor, then we withdraw.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02146
Aḥmad Amīn then points to the religious basis for this position in the Qurʾānic verse:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02147
“If two groups of believers fight one another, make peace between them. But if one of them attacks the other unjustly, then fight the aggressing group until it returns to the command of God.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02148
That explains the earlier “Muʿtazila.” But does the same political and historical line continue into the later Muʿtazila?
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02149
To answer this, we first need to understand the central idea around which the later group originally formed.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02150

Historically, the Muʿtazilite school is usually said to have begun with the disagreement between al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and his pupil Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ over the status of a Muslim who commits a major sin. Was such a person an unbeliever, or was he still a believer?
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02151
Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī regarded him as a “hypocrite.” Wāṣil, by contrast, regarded him as a “sinner.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02152

The first position meant that someone who committed a major sin did not possess complete faith, because he said one thing while concealing something else. That, according to this view, was what made him a hypocrite. He therefore deserved the punishment of an unbeliever in the afterlife.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02153

Wāṣil’s position meant something different. The sinner still possessed faith in the sense of inward belief, but by committing a major sin he violated the practical commands of the religious law. This was what made him a sinner.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02154
But what would happen to such a person in the afterlife?
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02155

Here Wāṣil introduced a new formula for describing the position of someone who had committed a major sin in relation to belief and unbelief. He argued that such a person occupied “a position between the two positions”: a middle position between believer and unbeliever. He was therefore neither fully a believer nor an unbeliever.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02156

In fact, the middle position that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ assigned to the person who commits a major sin also placed the Muʿtazila themselves between the two main groups involved in this dispute: the Kharijites and the Murjiʾites.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02157
The Kharijites declared the person who commits a major sin to be an unbeliever. For them, faith rested on two inseparable foundations: belief and action together.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02158
The Murjiʾites, by contrast, still regarded such a person as a believer. They defined faith as inward belief alone. Neither verbal confession nor outward action formed part of faith itself.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02159
The Muʿtazila therefore stood between two opposing extremes.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02160
This brings us back to our earlier question. Was the political and historical outlook of the first Muʿtazila in early Islam the same basic outlook that later shaped the rationalist Muʿtazila?
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02161
Here too, we find ourselves in full agreement with Aḥmad Amīn’s answer: yes.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02162

We have seen that the question of the person who commits a major sin became the central point of disagreement between al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and his pupil Wāṣil. It led Wāṣil to “withdraw” from his teacher and, at first, gave the later Muʿtazila their defining principle of “a position between the two positions.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02163
But what did this question actually mean? And whom did it concern in real life?
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02164

To answer that, we have to go back to the point when the Kharijites first used the issue to define faith, and then follow it forward to the disagreement between al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ in their religious and scholarly circle.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02165

Historically, the issue raised after the killing of ʿUthmān, the Battle of the Camel, and the Battle of Ṣiffīn concerned the same basic political conflict and the same kinds of people as it did when the question reappeared in a new form in the study circles of Basra roughly two-thirds of a century later.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02166

In other words, the question that appeared in al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī’s school at the end of the first Islamic century as a problem of religious belief and knowledge was simply a continuation of the same question that had appeared earlier in the century in political and religious form.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02167
This is why we believe Aḥmad Amīn is entirely right when he says that:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02168
“Although this question appears on the surface to be purely religious, beneath it lies something politically very serious.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02169
He then compares the later Muʿtazilite position with those of the Kharijites and the Murjiʾites, much as we have just done.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02170
The teachings of the Kharijites, he concludes, had major political consequences. They:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02171

“led the Kharijites to take an actively hostile and military position toward the Umayyads. In their view, the Umayyads committed major sins and were therefore unbelievers, just like idol worshippers. Their caliphate could not be recognized, because the first condition for being caliph was to be a believer. More than that, they had to be fought until they entered their doctrine”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02172
—meaning the Kharijite doctrine.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02173
Aḥmad Amīn also argues that the Murjiʾite position had political consequences of its own:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02174

“The most important was that they applied their theory to all the political and religious disputes that had taken place among the Muslims. Neither ʿUthmān and his supporters nor those who rebelled against him were unbelievers. Neither ʿAlī and his followers nor ʿĀʾisha and her followers at the Battle of the Camel had left Islam. Neither those who fought under ʿAlī’s banner nor those who fought under Muʿāwiya’s banner at Ṣiffīn were unbelievers. The natural result of this Murjiʾite view was that the Umayyad caliphs remained believers no matter how many major sins they committed, just as their enemies remained believers as well. Another result was that the Murjiʾites did not agree with the Kharijites in fighting the Umayyads and trying to overthrow their state, and so on.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02175
Finally, he turns to the later Muʿtazila and concludes that their view also:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02176

“carried serious political consequences, just like the two earlier positions. The Muʿtazila were forced to apply their theory to the actions carried out since conflict first broke out among the Muslims. Which side had been wrong: ʿUthmān or those who killed him? Who had been right at the Battle of the Camel: ʿAlī or ʿĀʾisha? And how should we judge those who directed the war at Ṣiffīn? Which of them had committed a major sin? Who could rightly be called a sinner?”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02177
3 — A Historical Conclusion Grounded in Reality
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02178
Everything we have discussed so far was meant to prepare the way for a conclusion about the Muʿtazila that seems to us historically beyond serious doubt.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02179

The Muʿtazilite school did not arise in isolation. Its roots lay in earlier intellectual movements, and those movements in turn had roots in the real development of Arab-Islamic society. This was an age full of conflict. At first, that conflict was political even when it appeared outwardly in purely religious form. Later, it increasingly took on both religious and intellectual forms.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02180

To underline the historical basis of this conclusion, we can point to two other modern researchers who approach the history of philosophy in a very different way from our own. Their approach is mainly descriptive and historical, and their method is the traditional academic one. Yet they too conclude that the name “Muʿtazila” goes back:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02181

“to a time before Wāṣil separated from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and that the origins of the Muʿtazila were political. They arose in the same atmosphere that produced the Shīʿa and the Kharijites. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib’s accession to the caliphate was the starting point for the most important political and intellectual currents in Islam, if not for all of them.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02182

After recounting the events from the killing of ʿUthmān to the Battle of the Camel, these two researchers mention the neutral position taken by “a considerable number of the Companions” toward the two fighting sides.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02183

They then quote al-Nawbakhtī’s account in The Shīʿite Sects, where he says that Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, Muḥammad ibn Maslama, and Usāma ibn Zayd “withdrew” from ʿAlī. They refused to fight him, but they also refused to fight alongside him. They were therefore “called the Muʿtazila, and they were the ancestors of all the later Muʿtazila.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02184
The two researchers conclude:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02185
“Everything we know about the Muʿtazila leads us to accept al-Nawbakhtī’s account.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02186
The historical evidence here is so strong that any researcher seriously committed to the truth must take it into account, whatever method or approach they happen to use.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02187
In the case of the origins of the Muʿtazila, this evidence leaves little room for any interpretation that tries to separate the movement from its real historical roots.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02188
Al-Shahrastānī gives us a useful picture of this evidence. While explaining the four principles around which Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ’s Muʿtazilism revolved, he writes:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02189

“The third principle is the doctrine of the position between the two positions. Its origin was this. A man entered upon al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said: ‘Imam of the faith, a group has appeared in our time that declares those who commit major sins to be unbelievers. For them, a major sin is an act of unbelief that takes a person outside the religious community. These are the Waʿīdiyya Kharijites. Another group places its hopes in those who commit major sins. For them, a major sin does no harm as long as faith is present, just as an act of obedience brings no benefit where unbelief is present. These are the Murjiʾites of the community. What belief should we hold on this question?’
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02190

“Al-Ḥasan began to think. But before he could answer, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: ‘I do not say that a person who commits a major sin is absolutely a believer, nor that he is absolutely an unbeliever. He is in a position between the two positions: neither believer nor unbeliever.’
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02191

“He then stood up and withdrew to one of the pillars of the mosque, where he began explaining his answer to a group of al-Ḥasan’s companions. Al-Ḥasan said: ‘Wāṣil has withdrawn from us.’ He and his followers were therefore called the Muʿtazila.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02192
Al-Shahrastānī’s version differs from the accounts given by other historians such as al-Baghdādī, al-Dīnawarī, al-Malaṭī, and al-Masʿūdī.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02193

But despite their differences over how the name “Muʿtazila” first arose, all these accounts point to the same basic conclusion: the principle of “a position between the two positions”—the Muʿtazilite doctrine concerning the person who commits a major sin—was closely tied to the emergence of the Muʿtazila as an intellectual school within Islamic theology.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02194
We have just seen that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ’s answer, which became one of the basic principles of Muʿtazilism, came in response to a question about the Kharijites and the Murjiʾites.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02195
And we know that both of those movements represented political positions toward a political struggle that was actually taking place around them.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02196

There can therefore be little doubt that Wāṣil’s theoretical principle concerning the person who commits a major sin did not arise separately from the reality of Arab-Islamic society and the political opinions, disputes, and positions that were then in fierce conflict within it.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02197
The Muʿtazilite principle may have taken an abstract theoretical form and acquired a specifically religious character, but its roots still lay in that reality.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02198

Later we will see the Muʿtazila enter into a struggle with their opponents that eventually became an actual bloody conflict, backed by the full machinery of the state during two successive periods of Abbasid rule.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02199

We will then see the force of Aḥmad Amīn’s conclusion that the Muʿtazilite position on the person who commits a major sin “carried serious political consequences.” For this reason, “the Muʿtazila were forced to apply their theory to the actions carried out since conflict first broke out among the Muslims”—first between the supporters of ʿUthmān and the supporters of ʿAlī, and later between the supporters of ʿAlī, the Umayyads, and the Kharijites.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02200
4 — The Muʿtazila Between the Qadarites and the Jahmites
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02201
Now that we have finished with these preliminary questions, we can turn to the heart of the matter: the principles that came together to form the fully developed Muʿtazilite school.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02202

The first thing we notice is that these principles developed out of a collection of earlier ideas and opinions. Some had formed the basis of the Qadarite movement, while others had formed the basis of the Jahmite movement.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02203
Early historians and scholars noticed this connection. They expressed it almost directly by sometimes calling the Muʿtazila “Qadarites” and at other times “Jahmites.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02204
Neither name was meaningless or arbitrary. And the Muʿtazila’s later rejection of both names was not meaningless or arbitrary either.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02205

Calling the Muʿtazila “Qadarites” made sense because belief in human freedom of choice—in both will and action—became one of the basic pillars of Muʿtazilite doctrine. This was also the principle on which the earlier Qadarite movement had been built.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02206

Calling them “Jahmites” also made sense because many of Jahm’s ideas became central parts of Muʿtazilite thought. These included his views on the attributes of God, the created nature of the Qurʾān, the rational basis of good and evil, and the rational interpretation of Islamic texts.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02207
At the same time, however, the Muʿtazila were also right to reject both labels.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02208
There were two reasons for rejecting the name “Qadarites.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02209
First, the name referred to only one part of Muʿtazilite doctrine. The earlier Qadarite belief in human freedom was important, but it was far from being the whole of Muʿtazilism.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02210
Second, it was fundamentally misleading to call the doctrine of free choice “Qadarism” in the first place.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02211
The Muʿtazila themselves objected to the label and argued that:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02212
“The term Qadarites applies to those who say that divine decree, both good and evil, comes from God Most High.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02213
They therefore rejected the name because they wanted to avoid the disgrace attached to it. The term had become widely condemned because of the saying attributed to the Prophet:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02214
“The Qadarites are the Magians of this community.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02215

The Muʿtazila also rejected the name “Jahmites” because one of Jahm’s best-known doctrines was belief in compulsion: the view that human beings do not freely choose their actions. The Muʿtazila held exactly the opposite position.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02216
As one source puts it:
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02217
“Jahm agreed with the Muʿtazila in denying the attributes, and went beyond them in other matters.”
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02218
But once we move beyond questions of labels and terminology, the basic historical fact remains.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02219
Muʿtazilism did not appear out of nothing, nor was it built on nothing.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02220
It grew out of earlier intellectual seeds. Those seeds developed rapidly because Qadarite and Jahmite ideas interacted in two different ways.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02221
On the question of human freedom and responsibility, they represented opposing positions and came into conflict with one another.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02222

Yet despite that disagreement, both movements also helped establish a rational approach to Islamic beliefs and a willingness to interpret Islamic texts through reason, even though each did so in a different direction.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02223

The Muʿtazilite movement as a whole therefore arose as the expression of a broader intellectual current with a particular way of understanding religious belief. It did not begin as a spontaneous act by one individual.
The Muʿtazila and the Muʿtazilite–Ashʿarite Conflict
passage-en-02224

For this reason, serious historical research cannot accept what might seem to follow from al-Shahrastānī’s story, or from similar accounts of the origins of the Muʿtazila and their name: that the movement first appeared as an individual act carried out by one man, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ.
